definition: The first small pour that saturates grounds and lets trapped CO2 escape, visible as bubbling. Skipping it can cause uneven extraction, since escaping gas otherwise pushes water away from the grounds.
The process of dissolving flavor compounds out of ground coffee into water. Under-extraction tastes sour and thin; over-extraction tastes bitter and harsh.
The ratio of coffee to water by weight, e.g. 1:16. Lower ratios (more coffee) produce a stronger, more concentrated cup.
Stirring, swirling, or turbulent pouring that increases contact between water and grounds, speeding up and evening out extraction.
Water finding a low-resistance path through the coffee bed instead of flowing evenly, causing some grounds to be over-extracted and others under-extracted.
The final phase where remaining water drains through the coffee bed. A drawdown that's much faster or slower than expected usually points to grind size.
Steeping grounds fully submerged in water for a set time, then separating them (French press, AeroPress), as opposed to water flowing continuously through a bed of grounds.
Water is poured over grounds and flows through a filter under gravity, extracting coffee as it passes rather than steeping in place.
The reddish-brown foam on top of a fresh espresso shot, formed from emulsified oils and CO2 released under pressure. It fades quickly, which is why espresso is served immediately.
How finely coffee is ground. Finer grinds increase extraction speed and resistance to water flow; coarser grinds slow it down. Each brew method has a rough target range.
Hotter water extracts faster and pulls out more soluble compounds. Most methods target 90–96°C (195–205°F); darker roasts are often brewed slightly cooler to avoid excess bitterness.

A measurement of how much dissolved coffee is in the final liquid, used by some brewers with a refractometer to dial in strength precisely. Not something you need for any of the recipes here — just useful to know if you see it mentioned elsewhere.
